q: A quantity of heat of 300 J is transferred to a gas, and the gas expands, doing 120 J of work on the piston. By how much does the internal energy of the gas change?
a: $Q = +300\,\text{J}$ and $W = -120\,\text{J}$, because the system does work on the surroundings. $\Delta U = 300\,\text{J} - 120\,\text{J} = 180\,\text{J}$, so the internal energy increases by 180 J.

q: Why is the sentence "a hot stone has a lot of heat in it" inaccurate in physics? What does the stone really have?
a: Heat is the transfer of energy because of a temperature difference, not a property of an object. The stone has internal energy and a high temperature; heat is transferred only when the stone touches a colder object.

q: Hot coffee has just been sealed in a thermos flask whose inner wall is still cool. The flask and its contents form an isolated system: no energy is transferred in or out, and no work is done on it. What happens to the internal energy of this system, and what can still happen to the internal energy of the coffee?
a: The internal energy of the flask and its contents stays constant, because no energy is transferred into or out of the system. Inside the system, energy is still transferred as heat from the coffee to the colder inner parts of the flask (the inner wall and the air) until the temperatures even out: the internal energy of the coffee decreases and that of the inner parts increases by the same amount.
